details.abstract: Long-horizon agents often keep revisiting how work was done, even when the results are already preserved in files and task state. We introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that enables agents to continue from reusable task progress rather than repeatedly compressing interaction histories. On OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus, CarryOn improves performance by 5.8 and 7.0 percentage points, while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. title: BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business

details.title: BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business
details.abstract: AI agents are moving from answering questions to executing business workflows, where actions change business states, commit resources, and shape later decisions. We introduce BizAgentBench, a long-horizon benchmark grounded in workflows from a global payments company. Agents complete tasks through customer dialogue, document retrieval, and tool use in a stateful simulated environment. Its design centers on three business insights. First, rule applicability depends on the business event. Guidance is scattered across manuals, FAQs, and operational notices. Historical and current instructions coexist, and apparent conflicts may reflect differences in product, region, or effective period. An expired insurance policy, for example, may still cover an incident that occurred during its coverage period. Agents must establish which sources are authoritative and which rules govern the event they are handling. Second, compliance depends on authorization and business state at the moment of execution. A customer’s general consent does not authorize every operation: approval must cover the specific action and its terms, come from someone with the required authority, and precede execution. A tool may accept an operation that breaches a reserve requirement or interrupts required coverage. Restoring the balance later does not erase the earlier violation; critical constraints must hold throughout the workflow. Third, waiting can make a task infeasible. Reviews, refunds, or settlements may finish after another obligation requires action. A priority delivery booking window, for example, may close before warehouse confirmation arrives, making timely delivery impossible if the agent waits. Agents must coordinate information gathering and action while accounting for shared resources and existing commitments. A locally reasonable decision can consume funds or time needed elsewhere. BizAgentBench translates these insights into deterministic checks of goal attainment, process compliance, and prohibited side effects, while accepting different valid strategies. GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.3% strict success, with just 40% of tasks completed successfully in all three runs. The benchmark brings evaluation closer to the demands of business execution: identifying the right rules, acting at the right time, and maintaining valid execution throughout.

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

details.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
details.abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We are excited to share TreeOPSD (Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning). Training long-horizon LLM agents with verifiable rewards faces two practical bottlenecks: terminal rewards alone make turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing remedies either add extra components (learned critics, process annotations, or stronger external teachers) or rely on importance-ratio clipping, which restricts step size without defining a finite target where updates should stop. TreeOPSD addresses both challenges in a critic-free, self-distillation framework. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, it branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each backed-up credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the turn-level likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the Forward KL divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the exact tree policy-gradient direction as its tangent at the behavior policy, while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Across Multi-Hop QA and Deep Research benchmarks (from 1.7B to 30B-A3B models), TreeOPSD consistently outperforms GRPO, GSPO, and fixed-credit tree policy gradients under matched rollout budgets, improving Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by +4.97 points on average in the Deep Research setting.

We explore two key directions in mobile agent research: 1. Scalable Training Environments. Existing emulator-based environments are heavyweight and cover limited apps, especially commercial ones. We introduce MobileGym++ , featuring 35 high-fidelity, fully controllable commercial-style apps with cross-app workflow, built through human–coding agent collaboration. Together with emulator-based apps, we provide an open playground of 110+ diverse apps for scalable data synthesis and agentic RL. You can try our apps directly on the project website! 2. Hybrid GUI & CLI. While hybrid computer use is gaining traction, mobile agents remain largely limited to GUI interactions. We explore a new setting where mobile apps expose app-native tools, enabling agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We also introduce MobileGym++ Bench , supporting both GUI-only and hybrid evaluation on challenging commercial-app tasks. OpenMobile-2 achieves competitive results on established benchmarks and nearly 2× performance on real-device mobile tasks . 🔥 Everything is open-source! title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI

details.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
details.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents

details.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We introduce OS-Helix , a computer-using agent trained to coordinate GUI interaction and code execution within a single policy. Desktop tasks often need both: the GUI exposes what users see, while code can work precisely with files and system state. Simply giving a GUI agent a code tool does not teach it when to use each one, so we train that coordination directly. We build reproducible desktop environments by pairing applications with authentic artifacts, generate verifiable tasks, and use filtered GUI/code trajectories for supervised training. We then train online with Step-balanced GSPO, which addresses optimization imbalance between GUI and code actions. OS-Helix-27B-RL reaches 66.44% on OSWorld-Verified and 63.87% on WindowsAgentArena, without Windows-specific training data. Project page · Models · Dataset . We’re organizing the training and evaluation code for release. We’d welcome your feedback and questions!

title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?

details.title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?
details.abstract: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on either real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve the complexity of natural scenes, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether the abilities measured in toy games correspond to those required in real-world visual reasoning, and whether game examples can provide useful signals for solving real-world tasks. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark for studying these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. On the game side, we construct 1,000 independently generated samples from executable task specifications and verify their answers programmatically. On the real-world side, we curate and construct 400 samples from diverse real-world sources. We connect the two settings according to shared reasoning requirements, including visual evidence, spatial operations, constraints, and state transitions, rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs across both settings. Performance on game and real-world tasks shows consistent cross-setting trends, with a Pearson correlation of 0.935 and a Spearman correlation of 0.935. We further examine game-to-real transfer through one-shot in-context learning on four models. The effect varies across capabilities and models. Constraint reasoning shows positive gains for several models, while fine-grained perception consistently declines with game demonstrations. These results show that toy games can reflect some reasoning patterns observed in real-world tasks and can provide useful demonstrations in selected settings. To further support model training, we construct Game2Real-Dataset, comprising nearly 24K game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. These samples are generated from executable task specifications and verified programmatically. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench .

title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models

details.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
details.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average 3.16× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average.

title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling

details.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
details.abstract: Existing geometry-based world models often rely on view-dependent features, entangling scene dynamics with camera-induced variations. GeoState addresses this by learning a view-decoupled scene state, allowing the world model to focus on scene dynamics while a camera-conditioned geometry decoder handles viewpoint-dependent observations. GeoState improves long-horizon depth forecasting on Waymo, enables geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Ablation studies further show that view decoupling improves state predictability compared to directly forecasting geometry foundation model features.

We find that goal grounding is the dominant failure in the VLM navigation policies we study. Explicit grounding improves performance across six benchmarks, while giving the same policy ground-truth grounding nearly closes the gap to the demonstration expert.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching

details.title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
details.abstract: TL;DR: An LLM's sparse autoencoder works as a shared coordinate system for matching symbols across heterogeneous systems (formal provers, code, table schemas, knowledge graphs, ontologies), with no training and no aligned pairs. How SAE-IDF works An LLM reads each symbol in its native context (e.g., a KG class with its instances, a Lean 4 statement). The SAE encodes the hidden states into a sparse code of named features. Each feature is weighted by its rarity (IDF, as in classic text retrieval), and candidates are ranked by cosine. Results Beats the same LLM's dense hidden states on all 12 tasks with Gemma-2-9B, and on all but one with Llama-3.1-8B Biggest gains where notations differ most: Lean 4 → Metamath 0.21 → 0.66 MRR, Lean 4 → HOL Light 0.54 → 0.90 Scales with the dictionary: HOL Light MRR rises from 0.82 to 0.94 as the SAE grows from 16k to 1M features Both ingredients matter: without IDF the SAE code mostly trails dense, and a random dictionary with the same IDF stays below dense on every task Interpretable by construction: the cosine decomposes exactly over features, so every match reads as a few named concepts. For example, in NELL trainstation → DBpedia RailwayStation , 93% of the match comes from two features about railroads and stations. A first step toward a universal symbolic backbone for neuro-symbolic models at LLM scale.

title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion

details.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
details.abstract: Introducing MT Forcing : towards stable and consistent multi-turn image editing with autoregressive diffusion. Image editing models often produce good results in a single turn, yet accumulate artifacts and lose previously established details over successive edits. MT Forcing addresses both visual degradation and content drift through two complementary training signals: Single-Turn DMD trains on student self-rollouts, using a teacher that applies cumulative editing instructions directly to the original image in one turn. Teacher-Forcing Guidance uses consistent reference trajectories for warmup and regularization, helping preserve content across turns. On MTEdit-Bench, applying MT Forcing to SenseNova-U1.5 improves eight-turn average instruction following from 8.47 to 9.66 and content consistency from 7.09 to 8.40 . Explore the project page for interactive comparisons and a 15-turn editing demo! 🤗 Model weights: https://huggingface.co/houyuanchen/MT-Forcing

title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents

details.title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents
details.abstract: 🚀 Excited to share our latest work: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents (SERA) ! As coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex increasingly adopt task decomposition and subagent delegation, recursive agent architectures are emerging as a promising paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks. However, effectively training recursive agents remains a fundamental challenge . While final task outcomes are often verifiable, the intermediate subtasks generated by agents lack ground-truth supervision, making it difficult to assign credit for subtask execution and even harder to evaluate decomposition quality. Existing approaches typically rely on external verifiers or LLM judges, which can be costly and provide limited supervision for learning effective decomposition. To address this challenge, we introduce SERA (Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents) , a framework that jointly trains a single policy to decompose, execute, and evaluate subtasks. SERA enables agents to generate task-specific evaluation rubrics before delegation and learns to align these rubrics with verifiable task outcomes, providing finer-grained feedback for subtask execution. We also introduce a Leaf-Coverage Reward to directly improve decomposition quality. 🔍 Our key finding: Learning to Evaluate Improves Solving. Because execution and evaluation share the same model parameters, training agents to recognize successful subtask outcomes also improves their ability to solve those subtasks . In other words, evaluation is not merely a source of supervision; it can itself become a learned capability that strengthens agent reasoning and execution. Experimentally, SERA outperforms strong recursive-agent baselines by 5.38 and 13.14 percentage points on TextCraft-Synth and TextWorld-Sync, respectively. Moreover, the learned rubrics can guide tree search at inference time, yielding an additional 2.43-point improvement on TextWorld-Sync. Our results suggest a broader perspective: rather than relying solely on external judges, we can train agents to evaluate their own work, and in doing so, make them better problem solvers.

title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents

details.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
details.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning learns only from a terminal scalar reward, so most of a long rollout goes unused. Per-step value targets all derive from that one scalar, and next-observation targets are long, noisy, and reach only one step ahead. CoPE adds multi-step action targets: on successful trajectories, the policy backbone is also trained to forecast the actions that follow each history, so acting and forecasting co-evolve in one model. At inference it still acts one step at a time, with no overhead. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, τ2-bench, and AppWorld, CoPE outperforms GRPO and predictive-auxiliary baselines with up to 2.0× the sample efficiency, using no extra models, pretraining stages, or inference-time cost.

title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent

details.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
details.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering. Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves. However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge. We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution. RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows. The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration. Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow .

title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds

details.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
details.abstract: This Perspective aims to establish latent-world understanding as a central goal for interpreting predictive world models. We note that decodability is not understanding: accessible information does not reveal how it is organized, evolves, or causally supports prediction. Building on this observation, we envision the Ground–Structure–Verify–Act blueprint as a path toward this goal, and as a framework for shaping future research on latent-world interpretability. We call for future interpretability efforts to move beyond isolated representation-level analyses toward systematically understanding, validating, and acting on the internal worlds learned by predictive models.

details.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
details.abstract: How can we build training environments for AI coworkers that need to use tools, handle multi-turn interactions, and operate in changing workspaces? We introduce CoworkEnv, a framework that synthesizes executable environments for training these agents. It combines capability-guided task generation with programmatic validation and feedback-based repair, supporting both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using CoworkEnv, we train compact PocketWorker models. On Claw-Eval, SFT improves Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 46.6 to 64.1 (+17.5 points), with a +31.9-point gain on multi-turn tasks. We welcome feedback and discussion on environment synthesis and training long-horizon agents!

title: PAR: Progress-Aligned Recurrence for Length Generalization in State Tracking

details.title: PAR: Progress-Aligned Recurrence for Length Generalization in State Tracking
details.abstract: 🚀 Introducing PAR, our new work on length extrapolation in looped language models. 📦 The task is simple: five boxes, one object in each. Follow a sequence of swaps, then answer what’s inside. We train the model on short sequences and test whether it can keep up as the sequences get much longer. Simply running more loops is not enough: performance breaks down at just 2× the training length. Scaling up the model alone doesn’t solve the problem either. On single-query S5, fixed-depth Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 7B achieve only around 20% accuracy at 16× the training length—roughly random guessing. We identify two key obstacles: supervising only the final answer leaves the model without clear guidance on how far to advance in each loop; repeatedly applying the same layers hundreds of times causes the hidden-state scale to drift. 💡 PAR makes two straightforward changes: at loop k, predict the state after the first k steps; after each loop, rescale the hidden states to match their scale in the first loop. This aligns the loops with task progress: one loop, one step. 📈 On swap-S5, a 0.5B model trained on sequences of at most 32 steps achieves 95.5% full-state accuracy at 512 steps—a 16× length extrapolation. For comparison, the previous best method, RLT, achieves 55.7%, while the same model using chain-of-thought (CoT) reaches just 0.8%. On single-query S5, PAR substantially outperforms fixed-depth models at every tested size, spanning Qwen2.5 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, and 7B, and Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 4B. Across all four Qwen2.5 sizes, the best training runs achieve 100% accuracy at 16× the training length. The model can also learn when to stop. We further show that PAR can be trained with final-answer supervision alone, without intermediate-state annotations.

title: Large Flow Language Models

details.title: Large Flow Language Models
details.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.

title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding

details.title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
details.abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. To break this loop, in this paper, we propose Compressed Window Auto-Regression (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.

Core contributions: Worlds: persona-driven, multi-day personal computers where websites, MCP services, and local files share one state, so agents can combine GUI, MCP, and CLI, and the whole pipeline is powered by open-source models, without any reliance on proprietary frontier models. Tasks: execution-based quality gates (heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes) keep tasks solvable, challenging, and reliably verified. We release 341 environment–task pairs; some need over 100 agent steps, and GPT-6-Astra solves only about 60%. Results: trained exclusively in these synthetic worlds, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-4B improve on all 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, by +10.58 and +8.21 points on average. title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills

details.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
details.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SKILLTRANSFERBENCH, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort

title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: Excited to share our work Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning ! Most existing agentic RL methods train through a single fixed harness, potentially limiting generalization across different execution configurations. We introduce Harness Scaling , a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that focuses on how agents execute , complementing traditional scaling over tasks and environments. Our approach organizes harness diversity through five components (system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, and workflow), combining structured configuration selection with cross-harness RL. Key findings: Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen harness configurations across models, benchmarks, and RL algorithms. Structured harness selection and locality-aware training are more effective than simply increasing the number of training configurations. Remarkably, training across diverse white-box harnesses transfers effectively to unseen black-box harnesses such as Claude Code, even outperforming direct black-box RL training. Our results highlight that not only harness diversity, but how it is organized, matters for generalizable agentic RL. Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation

details.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
details.abstract: 🔥🔥🔥Which spectral channels matter, and where? SSI explains a model score with signed attributions for each spatial cell and channel. It keeps the surrounding image fixed while allocating a cell's contribution among its channels using Shapley values. A channel's contribution can change across an image. SSI asks how the channels within one spatial cell affect the chosen model score, conditioned on the observed values of all other cells. ✅ SSI has the best reported mean for all three metrics on all three datasets under both masking baselines. For example, mean-baseline HLS joint deletion is .1545 for SSI versus .2096 for KernelSHAP, the strongest non-SSI method on that metric. ✅ SSI leads the compared methods in spatial localization, spectral Hit@K, and channel deletion across the evaluated datasets.

title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams

details.title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
details.abstract: 🚀 We present GRSE (Group-Relative Skill Evolution), a framework that tackles a fundamental question in multi-agent learning: When a team succeeds or fails, which agent's skill should actually change? Instead of rewarding all skills involved in successful trajectories, GRSE performs group-relative credit assignment across multiple executions to identify the skills that truly drive outcomes. Key highlights: 🎯 Assigns credit at the agent-skill level 🔍 Identifies causal contributors through trajectory comparison 🤝 Supports continual multi-agent skill evolution 📈 Outperforms existing skill-learning methods on HotpotQA and LoCoMo 🛡️ Remains robust under noisy and corrupted skill libraries We believe GRSE is an important step toward scalable and self-improving multi-agent systems. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27227 💻 Code: https://github.com/yananma1029/GRSE-Skills

title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience

details.title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
details.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.

title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models

details.title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
details.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation. Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors. Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation. We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources. After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6. The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra's 73.68. Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios. These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.

title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers

details.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
details.abstract: We introduce ALLOT, a training-free sparsity allocation method for block-sparse attention in video Diffusion Transformers. Our approach estimates each layer–step cell’s final-video sensitivity and jointly allocates densities under a measured-latency budget. At matched or shorter wall-clock time, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain over XAttention’s default on HunyuanVideo and outperforms or ties the defaults in all nine settings across four additional published pipelines.

title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models

details.title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models
details.abstract: World models often predict and plan over the tokens of a frozen visual encoder, so the encoder determines what they can see. We introduce ALPS (A Language-aligned, Pixel-renderable State encoder), a ViT-B/16 pretrained from scratch using only still images and text. A single set of frozen patch tokens supports physical-state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction . We first establish language, pixel, and spatial capabilities through joint pretraining, then strengthen state representations via cross-view self-distillation. Key results: State: Lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B encoders (compared with 15 public encoders), matching the 3.5× larger V-JEPA 2-L. Language: Strong native language alignment, achieving 93.2% Flickr30k and 70.2% COCO image-to-text Recall@1. Pixels: Accurate pixel reconstruction from frozen tokens, including direct rendering of predicted world-model futures. Control & Planning: Highest mean LIBERO policy success (85.5%) with its native text tower; matches or exceeds leading encoders on PushT, Wall, and Granular. Open release: Both checkpoints (Stage 1 & ALPS), eight LIBERO policies, and JAX / PyTorch training and evaluation code. 🌐 Project: https://ucsc-vlaa.github.io/ALPS/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/ALPS 🤗 Weights: https://huggingface.co/UCSC-VLAA/ALPS

title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training

details.title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training
details.abstract: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output.

title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents

details.title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
details.abstract: TL DR: LLM agents often re-issue a tool call they already made and get the same observation back. We call this a loop . DeLoop turns each loop into a free training pair from the agent's own rollout: the repeated call is the rejected action, and the agent's first later loop-breaking action is the chosen one. We train on these pairs with DPO. No task reward, gold answer, or LLM judge needed. Why it matters: loops get much worse when the history is compressed. On CodeGym, Qwen3-8B loops in 29.0% of runs with the full history and in 57.3% under summarization. Summaries that explicitly track past actions don't fix it, because the agent often ignores a record it already has. Results Qwen3-8B on CodeGym: loop rate 57.3% → 6.1% (9.4×), steps per task 15.0 → 4.7 , tokens −47%, with similar task success Qwen3-14B / 32B: task success +7.2 / +7.1 points (45.1 → 52.3 , 37.7 → 44.8 ) With cross-domain pairs (DeLoop-Mix): Qwen3-8B success 25.1 → 30.3 . Loops also drop under 7 memory policies, in ALFWorld, Open-AgentRL, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BrowseComp-Plus (22.4% → 1.2%) 🔗 Project page (with an interactive example of a loop forming): https://cskyl.github.io/deloop/ 📄 arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19376 💻 Code and data: coming soon at https://github.com/cskyl/deloop

title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting

details.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
details.abstract: What does it take for AI agents to continuously improve themselves? We argue that the environment is not merely a place for training or evaluation, but a fundamental driver of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We introduce DeepEvolve, a system in which agents co-evolve with a living environment that continually generates new, verifiable real-world event prediction tasks, adapts to the agent’s weaknesses, and provides feedback for sustained capability growth. Through parameter-level learning and reusable skill evolution, DeepEvolve turns experience into lasting improvements while addressing information leakage in open-world learning. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in real-world event prediction, highlighting evolving environments as a key foundation for self-improving AI.

title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift

details.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
details.abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally

details.title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
details.abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of some (not all) and or (not both) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.

title: Making MLLM Latents Matter: Factor-Aware Predictive Learning for Cinematic Video Generation

details.title: Making MLLM Latents Matter: Factor-Aware Predictive Learning for Cinematic Video Generation
details.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.

title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE

details.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
details.abstract: A comparison between the Vanilla and Meta-Expert models shows that, when trained under the optimal settings of the Vanilla model at varying depths and scales, models with Meta Experts achieve loss comparable to the Vanilla baselines while using only 70–80% as many experts, or 75–90% as many parameters. Notably, the savings in both experts and parameters grow as the models become deeper and larger, demonstrating the favorable scalability of Meta Experts. The proposed method has been scaled up in Intern-S2-Mobius, which is available at https://github.com/InternLM/Intern-S2-Mobius and https://huggingface.co/internlm/Intern-S2-Mobius .

details.title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V
details.abstract: We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a comprehensive benchmark for general-purpose code-based video generation across text-to-video, image-to-video, and video-to-video settings. The benchmark comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories and 24 subtypes, covering scene construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. We evaluate 15 MLLMs using complementary objective metrics and MLLM-based judgments, revealing substantial performance gaps across input settings and task complexities, as well as a disconnect between visual quality and execution reliability. We welcome feedback and discussion!

details.title: Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? Naive RAG Is Stronger Than We Thought
details.abstract: RAW-RAG challenges the necessity of complex agentic memory for long-term conversation understanding. By combining dense retrieval and reranking over raw history, it ranks first among compared memory systems in six of seven settings across four benchmarks. Its analyses highlight evidence coverage and relational completeness as key drivers of performance, establishing naive RAG as an essential baseline.

title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models

details.title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models
details.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.
